implementation_notes: Rust makes the guardian structural rather than conventional: `Mutex<T>` owns the value it protects and its documentation states that the data 'can only be accessed through the RAII guards returned from lock and try_lock', so the borrow checker rejects any attempt to read `T` without holding the guard and the lock cannot be forgotten. The shared handle is `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (or `&Mutex<T>`), and the canonical shape is a struct whose methods lock, mutate and let the `MutexGuard` drop - the tokio documentation names exactly this: wrap the `Arc<Mutex<..>>` in a struct, provide methods and lock only inside them. The standard library adds poisoning as a safety net (a panic while holding the lock makes later `lock()` calls return `Err`, which you either propagate or deliberately recover from with `into_inner`), and `RwLock`, atomics or a channel-owned actor are the alternatives chosen inside the same wrapper.
pitfalls: Holding a `MutexGuard` across `.await` or across a blocking call turns the guardian into a deadlock source; the guard must live only inside the synchronous critical section (the tokio docs warn that the compiler will not always catch it).
Poisoning is part of the contract: `.unwrap()` propagates a panic from another thread, `into_inner()` accepts possibly inconsistent state - pick one deliberately instead of mixing them.
`Arc<Mutex<T>>` keeps the state alive as long as any clone exists, so caching handles, listeners or tasks that hold clones keeps the guardian (and its lock) alive indefinitely.

variants.name: tokio::sync::Mutex held across await points
variants.implementation_notes: When the guarded work must await - typically an I/O resource such as a database connection behind the lock - `tokio::sync::Mutex` is the guardian: `lock()` yields instead of blocking a runtime thread, the guard is designed to be held across `.await`, and acquisition is FIFO. Tokio's own guidance is to use it only for that case: for plain data the standard-library mutex is preferred because the async mutex is more expensive and the blocking guard must never cross an await point. The struct-wrapper idiom stays the same, with `async fn` methods instead of `fn`.
pitfalls: The async mutex is not a substitute for the blocking one: holding it across a long computation serialises the whole task set, and its guard must not be stored in a struct that outlives the await.
Unlike `std::sync::Mutex`, a panic does not poison it - the mutex is unlocked and possibly inconsistent state is left behind, so invariants must be re-established by the caller.
